moduleTitle: The promised land and the Covenant with Abraham

note.specFocus: The Covenant and the mitzvot: the promised land and the Covenant with Abraham, Genesis 12:1–3 (prescribed text), and its importance for Jews today.
note.summary:
What is a covenant?
A covenant (brit) is a binding agreement between God and people, with promises and responsibilities on both sides. Judaism understands the relationship between God and the Jewish people as a covenant relationship.

Abraham
Abraham (first called Abram) lived about 4,000 years ago in Mesopotamia (Ur, then Haran). Jewish tradition says he came to recognise that there is only one God and rejected the idols of his father Terah. He is called Avraham Avinu, "Abraham our father", the first of the patriarchs (Abraham, Isaac and Jacob).

The prescribed text: Genesis 12:1–3
"The Lord said to Abram: Go forth from your land, from your birthplace and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you. I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great, and you shall be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and curse him that curses you; and all the families of the earth shall be blessed through you."
God's promises:
1. Land: "the land that I will show you", later identified as Canaan (Genesis 12:7; 15:18).
2. Nation: Abram's descendants will become "a great nation".
3. Blessing: Abraham will be blessed and will be a blessing, and all the families of the earth will be blessed through him.
Abraham's part: faith and obedience. He leaves everything and goes, trusting God.

The covenant develops
• Genesis 15: the "covenant between the pieces". God promises descendants as many as the stars and the land "from the river of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates".
• Genesis 17: God changes Abram's name to Abraham ("father of many nations") and gives the sign of the covenant: circumcision of every male at eight days old (brit milah), "an everlasting covenant". God promises "all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession" (17:8).
• Genesis 22 (the binding of Isaac, the Akedah) is the supreme test of Abraham's faith. It is read on Rosh Hashanah.

The promised land
• Eretz Yisrael, the land of Israel, is central to Jewish identity. Jews pray facing Jerusalem, and many end the Pesach seder and Yom Kippur with "Next year in Jerusalem".
• After centuries of exile, the modern State of Israel was founded in 1948. Its Law of Return (1950) allows any Jew to settle there.
• Views differ. Many Jews see Israel as the fulfilment of God's promise; others, including many secular Zionists, see it in historical and political terms. Some strictly Orthodox groups believe a Jewish state should wait for the Messiah. Many Reform Jews value Israel deeply while stressing the universal side of the covenant ("all families of the earth shall be blessed").
• Many Jews disagree about Israeli government policies; supporting the land is not the same as supporting every political decision.

Importance today
• Brit milah continues the sign of the covenant for Jewish boys today.
• Jews see themselves as the descendants of Abraham, with a responsibility to be "a blessing" through ethical living.
• Abraham is a model of faith, of hospitality (Genesis 18, welcoming three strangers) and of justice (arguing for Sodom, Genesis 18:25).

Key terms: brit (covenant); Avraham Avinu; patriarchs; Eretz Yisrael; brit milah; Akedah; Zionism.

questions.question:
Which one of the following did God promise Abram in Genesis 12:1–3?
A That he would become king of Egypt
B That he would become a great nation
C That he would build the Temple
D That he would receive the Ten Commandments
questions.modelAnswer: B – a great nation. In Genesis 12:2 God says, "I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you." Moses, not Abraham, received the Ten Commandments, and Solomon built the Temple.
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Write only the letter of the answer you choose; one mark is for the correct term or fact.

questions.question:
What was the sign of the covenant God gave Abraham in Genesis 17?
A The rainbow
B Shabbat
C Circumcision
D The tefillin
questions.modelAnswer: C – circumcision (brit milah) of every male at eight days old (Genesis 17:10–12). The rainbow was the sign of the covenant with Noah, and Shabbat is called a sign of the Sinai covenant.
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Write only the letter of the answer you choose; one mark is for the correct term or fact.

questions.question: Give two promises God made to Abraham.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any two from:
• Land ("the land that I will show you" or Canaan).
• Many descendants or a great nation.
• Blessing.
• A great name.
• All the families of the earth will be blessed through him.
• God will be their God for ever (Genesis 17:7).
questions.examTip: Give two separate, accurate points; short phrases are enough. Do not spend time explaining, and do not repeat the same idea in different words.

questions.question: Give two ways in which the Covenant with Abraham is important for Jews today.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any two from:
• Boys are circumcised at brit milah as a sign of the covenant.
• It gives Jews a special relationship with God.
• It is the basis of the Jewish link to the land of Israel.
• Abraham is a role model of faith and obedience.
• It gives Jews a duty to be a blessing to others.
• It is the origin of the Jewish people.
questions.examTip: Give two separate, accurate points; short phrases are enough. Do not spend time explaining, and do not repeat the same idea in different words.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which the Covenant with Abraham influences Jews today.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Through brit milah. God told Abraham that circumcision would be "the sign of the covenant" in every generation (Genesis 17:10–12). Jewish parents today have their baby sons circumcised on the eighth day in a ceremony, welcoming the child into the covenant that began with Abraham. Orthodox and most Reform families keep this practice.

2. Through their relationship with the land of Israel. God promised Abraham "the land that I will show you", the land of Canaan. Many Jews feel a deep connection to Israel as the promised land: they pray facing Jerusalem, visit it, support Israeli charities, and some make aliyah (emigrate) there under the Law of Return. Many see this connection as part of God's covenant promise.
questions.examTip: Make two distinct points. Develop each one (a simple point earns 1 mark, a detailed one 2 marks) by saying how or why it shapes what Jews believe or do today. If the question asks for contrasting ways, make sure the two are genuinely different, for example Orthodox and Reform.

questions.question: Explain two contrasting Jewish views about the importance of the promised land today.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Many Orthodox and Religious Zionist Jews believe the modern State of Israel is the fulfilment of God's covenant promise to Abraham that his descendants would inherit the land (Genesis 17:8). They see living in or supporting Israel as a religious duty, and some regard the state as "the first flowering of our redemption".

2. Some strictly Orthodox groups, such as Neturei Karta, believe that the Jewish return to the land should happen only when the Messiah comes. They therefore oppose a secular Jewish state, while still valuing the holiness of the land. Many Reform Jews take a different approach: they support Israel, but they emphasise the universal part of the covenant, that "all the families of the earth" will be blessed, and see Jewish life outside Israel, for example in Britain, as fully valid.
evidence: Prayer for the State of Israel

questions.question: Explain two promises that God made to Abraham in the covenant. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. The promise of land. God told Abram, "Go forth from your land… to the land that I will show you" (Genesis 12:1), and later promised "all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession" (Genesis 17:8). This is the origin of the Jewish belief that Eretz Yisrael is the promised land, which is why Jews pray facing Jerusalem.

2. The promise of a great nation and blessing. God said, "I will make of you a great nation… and all the families of the earth shall be blessed through you" (Genesis 12:2–3). Although Abraham and Sarah were old and childless, God promised descendants as many as the stars (Genesis 15:5), fulfilled through Isaac and Jacob. Jews see themselves as these descendants, with a responsibility to be a blessing to the wider world.
questions.examTip: Two developed beliefs or teachings (up to 2 marks each) plus 1 mark for a relevant reference to sacred writings or another source of Jewish teaching, such as the Torah, Tenakh, Talmud or Mishnah. Name the source clearly; it does not have to be word-for-word.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which Abraham showed his part in the covenant. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Faith and obedience in leaving his home. When God commanded, "Go forth from your land, from your birthplace and from your father's house" (Genesis 12:1), Abram left everything without knowing where he was going. Jews see this as the model of trust in God, and Genesis 15:6 says Abraham "believed in the Lord".

2. Accepting circumcision and passing faith to his descendants. In Genesis 17 Abraham circumcised himself and all the males of his household as the sign of the covenant. He was later willing even to offer his son Isaac (the Akedah, Genesis 22), showing complete obedience; God stopped him and renewed the promises. Jews continue Abraham's side of the covenant through brit milah and by bringing up children to follow God.

questions.question:
"The Covenant with Abraham is the most important covenant for Jews."

Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Jewish teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

The Covenant with Abraham is the beginning of the Jewish people. In Genesis 12:1–3 God calls Abram, promises him land, a great nation and blessing, and Abram responds with faith. Without this covenant there would be no descendants of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and so no Israelites at Sinai. Jews call him Avraham Avinu, "Abraham our father", which shows how basic he is to their identity.

The covenant is still marked physically today. God told Abraham that circumcision would be an "everlasting covenant" (Genesis 17:13), and Jewish boys are still circumcised at eight days old. The promise of land also links Jews to Israel today: many see the 1948 State of Israel and the Law of Return as connected to the promise of the land of Canaan.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

Many Jews would argue that the Covenant at Sinai is more important. At Sinai God gave the Torah and the Ten Commandments to the whole people, not one family, and Israel became "a kingdom of priests and a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6). The 613 mitzvot, which shape every part of Jewish life from Shabbat to kashrut, come from Sinai. Judaism is a way of life based on the Torah, so the covenant that gave the Torah could be seen as the most important.

It can also be argued that the covenants should not be ranked, because they form one developing relationship. Sinai fulfils the promises to Abraham: his descendants become a nation, are given laws, and are led towards the promised land. Reform Jews may stress the ethical and universal side of both covenants rather than choosing between them.

Some point out that the land promise is controversial in modern politics, while the moral law of Sinai unites Jews more widely.

JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION

The Covenant with Abraham is the foundation, because it creates the people and the promise. Sinai, however, gives that people its way of life through the Torah, and most Jews today experience their faith through keeping the mitzvot. The strongest conclusion is that Abraham's covenant is the most important in origin but the Sinai covenant is the most important in practice, and that Jews see them as two stages of one covenant rather than as rivals.
questions.examTip: Argue both sides with Jewish teaching, explain why each argument matters (do not just list views), weigh them, and finish with a conclusion that follows from what you have written. Include Orthodox and Reform views where they differ. Spelling, punctuation and grammar are also assessed on 12-mark answers.

questions.question:
"The promised land is still the most important part of God's covenant with the Jews."

Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Jewish teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

The land is central to the promises in Genesis. God's first words to Abram are a command to go "to the land that I will show you" (Genesis 12:1), and the land is promised again and again as "an everlasting possession" (Genesis 17:8). For centuries of exile Jews prayed facing Jerusalem, mourned the loss of the Temple on Tisha B'Av, and ended the seder with "Next year in Jerusalem".

For many Jews the land is still vital today. The founding of the State of Israel in 1948 gave Jews a homeland and a place of safety after the Holocaust, and the Law of Return allows any Jew to settle there. Religious Zionists see Israel as the start of redemption, and many British Jews visit, study there or make aliyah. Many mitzvot, such as some agricultural laws, can only be kept in the land itself.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

Many Jews would argue that the Torah and the mitzvot are more important than the land. Judaism survived nearly 2,000 years without a Jewish state, because the covenant was carried in the Torah, the synagogue and the home. The rabbis taught that the Shekhinah went into exile with the people, so the relationship with God is not dependent on land.

Reform Judaism has historically placed less emphasis on the return to the land. It stresses the ethical mission of being "a blessing" to "all the families of the earth" (Genesis 12:3) wherever Jews live. Some strictly Orthodox Jews believe the land should be restored only by the Messiah, and so they see the modern state as premature. Many Jews also feel that the present Israeli–Palestinian conflict makes it important not to make the land the whole of the covenant, and they emphasise justice and peace.

Others would say the relationship with God itself, "I will be your God" (Genesis 17:7), is the heart of the covenant, and that the land is one of several gifts within it.

JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION

The land is a very important part of the covenant, and for many Orthodox and Zionist Jews it is central. However, Jewish history shows that the covenant survived and flourished without the land, through Torah and mitzvot. The more convincing view is that the relationship with God and the keeping of the Torah are the heart of the covenant, and the land is a precious but not the most important part of it.
